steps.label: The two faulty assumptions
lines: Real gases deviate because two assumptions of
1) The molecular volume is NOT negligible —
at high pressure the gas is squeezed until the
molecules' own volume is a real share of the
at low temperature and high pressure the
molecules are slow and close, so the attractions
reduce the pressure on the walls.
steps.why: The ideal gas laws follow from point-size, non-attracting molecules. Each deviation of a real gas traces back to one of those two idealisations breaking down when molecules are pushed close together or slowed down.
common_mistakes: Giving only one of the two reasons. Volume AND attraction are separate marked points.
Saying real gases deviate at all conditions. At low pressure and high temperature they are nearly ideal.
steps.memory_tip: Two false assumptions of the ideal model: no size, no attraction. Both show up when the gas is cold and compressed.
steps.margin_note: State the failing condition with each reason: high P for volume, low T and high P for attraction.

steps.label: Measuring the deviation with Z
lines: The deviation is measured by the compressibility

lines.text: Ideal gas: Z = 1.  Real gas: Z < 1 when attraction dominates, Z > 1 when molecular volume dominates

lines: The van der Waals equation corrects for both:
(P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT — a for attraction,
steps.why: Z packs the whole comparison into one number, and the van der Waals equation repairs the two failures one term each — the a-term restores the pressure lost to attraction, the b-term removes the volume the molecules occupy.
common_mistakes: Swapping the Z < 1 and Z > 1 cases.
Assigning a to volume and b to attraction. a is attraction, b is volume.
steps.memory_tip: a for attraction — the letter matches. b is the bulk of the molecules.
steps.margin_note: This card joins the two asked VSAQs (Z and the van der Waals equation) into one story.
